summary: Addresses internationalization of HTML, extending the specification and giving recommendations for proper support of many languages and character sets. It is now historic and was replaced by RFC 2854.

plainLanguage.summary: This helps web pages show every language correctly. Letters from any language should look right.

what is unicode and why does html use it
how do you specify language in html

subtitle: Extending HTML to support every language and writing system in the world.

tldr.problem: HTML 2.0 was restricted to ISO-8859-1 (Latin-1), which supports only Western European languages. Pages in other languages had to use ad-hoc workarounds, creating interoperability problems and limiting the web's global reach.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 2070 changes HTML's document character set from ISO-8859-1 to ISO 10646 (Unicode), allowing any language or script. It adds a LANG attribute to all elements, a DIR attribute for bidirectional text (mixing left-to-right and right-to-left scripts), and elements like BDO, Q, SUP, and SUB for language-specific rendering. It specifies how character encoding is declared and negotiated.
tldr.outcome: This RFC is now Historic, superseded by RFC 2854 and later standards. However, it established the foundation for multilingual web support, and HTML has remained Unicode-based since.

today: RFC 2070 is now Historic, superseded by RFC 2854 (HTML 4.01). However, Unicode (ISO 10646) remains the standard document character set for HTML and the Web. Its internationalization features (LANG, DIR, BIDI support) are still in use, and all modern web frameworks build on the foundation this RFC established.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
Internationalization of HTML addresses the problem that HTML was built for Western European languages only. RFC 2070 removes the restriction to ISO-8859-1 by adopting the Universal Character Set (UCS) of ISO 10646, also known as Unicode.

The key insight is that the character encoding used to transmit a document (e.g., UTF-8, ISO-2022-JP) is separate from the abstract document character set used by HTML. The reference processing model decodes the external encoding to the document character set before parsing. This allows documents in any language to be interoperable while using any efficient encoding.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of being locked to one language's letters, HTML can now handle every language in the world. A page can mix languages, and everything should display correctly.

sections.title: The Document Character Set
sections.content:
RFC 2070 specifies that the HTML document character set is ISO 10646-1:1993 (Unicode). This is a superset of every other character set, including ISO-8859-1, so all existing HTML documents remain valid. Numeric character references now range from 1 to 2,147,483,645 instead of 0 to 255.

The external character encoding (how bytes are transmitted) is declared separately: via the HTTP Content-Type header's charset parameter (e.g., charset=ISO-2022-JP for Japanese), or via a META element in the document head. When no charset is declared, ISO-8859-1 is assumed for backwards compatibility, but servers are encouraged to always specify the correct encoding.

For transmission in UCS-2 or UCS-4, big-endian byte order is recommended, with an optional byte-order mark (ZERO-WIDTH NON-BREAKING SPACE) at the start. UTF-8 and UTF-7 are also supported as efficient encodings of Unicode.
sections.plainLanguage: Internally, HTML uses Unicode, which covers all languages. When you send the page on the network, you can use any efficient encoding, and the browser figures out which one it is.

sections.title: Language and Directionality Markup
sections.content:
The LANG attribute is added to all elements (except BR, HR, BASE, NEXTID, and META) to specify the natural language of content. Language tags follow RFC 1766: a primary tag (e.g., en, fr, ja) optionally followed by subtags (e.g., en-US, zh-Hans). Language tags are hierarchical: a user agent looking for en-US styles will match en-US first, then plain en, then use defaults.

The DIR attribute specifies text directionality as LTR (left-to-right) or RTL (right-to-left). This is critical for scripts like Arabic and Hebrew that read right-to-left. The BDO (Bidirectional Override) element forces directionality of its content, overriding the intrinsic directionality of characters. Left-to-right and right-to-left marks (LRM and RLM) are zero-width characters for disambiguating neutral characters like punctuation.
sections.plainLanguage: You can tag any part of a page with its language (like LANG=ja for Japanese) so the browser can render it correctly. The DIR attribute says if text goes left-to-right or right-to-left, which matters for Arabic, Hebrew, and other languages.

sections.title: Language-Specific Features
sections.content:
RFC 2070 adds the Q element for quotations, which browsers can render with appropriate quotation marks for the language (curved double quotes in English, guillemets in French, etc.). The SUP and SUB elements support superscripts and subscripts, which are necessary for languages like French where abbreviations use superscript text.

The ALIGN attribute is extended with a JUSTIFY value for languages where text justification is important. Form elements gain an ACCEPT-CHARSET attribute to declare which character encodings the server can handle, so the browser can warn users or limit input to compatible characters.

The zero-width joiner (ZWJ) and zero-width non-joiner (ZWNJ) control cursive joining in languages like Arabic and Persian, where whether letters join together affects their shape. These can be included as named entities or character references.
sections.plainLanguage: Different languages need different quotation marks, spacing, and text decoration. HTML now has ways to mark these up so browsers can render them properly for each language.

sections.title: Bidirectional Text and Complex Scripts
sections.content:
Bidirectional (BIDI) text occurs when left-to-right and right-to-left scripts are mixed in a single document, which is common in multilingual pages. The RFC follows the Unicode BIDI algorithm, which assigns directionality to each character and reorders them for display.

Text is stored in logical order (the order written and spoken) but displayed in visual order (the order on screen). The DIR attribute on block elements sets the base directionality. On inline elements, it creates a new embedding level, allowing nested directionality overrides. Without markup, ambiguous characters (like punctuation between Arabic and Latin text) may render incorrectly; directional marks (LRM, RLM) disambiguate them.

Complex scripts like Devanagari, Thai, and Khmer require glyph shaping (combining multiple characters into a single displayed shape). The LANG attribute helps renderers choose the correct glyph shapes for the language.
sections.plainLanguage: When you mix Arabic and English on the same line, your browser needs to know which way each part should go. Language tags and special marks help the browser figure this out and display it correctly.

sections.title: Form Submission and Encoding
sections.content:
HTML 2.0 form submission using application/x-www-form-urlencoded is problematic for non-ASCII text because URLs are restricted to ASCII characters. RFC 2070 recommends using multipart/form-data (from RFC 1867) with the POST method, which allows each form field to declare its own character encoding.

A CHARSET attribute on A and LINK elements hints at the character encoding of the linked resource, aiding user agents in navigating across pages with different encodings. The charset should match the MIME Content-Type header of the linked resource, but when missing, the hint helps browsers avoid encoding errors.
sections.plainLanguage: When you submit a form, the browser needs to know what character encoding the server expects. Multipart/form-data is more reliable than the old form encoding because it lets each field specify its own encoding.
